notes.definition: Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that help to cure bacterial diseases by killing infective bacteria inside the body. Painkillers and other medicines treat the symptoms of a disease but do not kill the pathogen that causes it.
explanation: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria (or stop them growing) inside the body. Penicillin was the first widely used antibiotic. Because antibiotics kill the pathogen itself, they actually cure a bacterial infection rather than just making the patient feel better. Since antibiotics came into use in the 1940s they have greatly reduced the number of deaths from infectious bacterial diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis and infected wounds.

Different antibiotics work against different bacteria. It is important that specific bacteria are treated with specific antibiotics: a doctor may need to identify which bacterium is causing an infection so that an antibiotic that is effective against that type of bacterium can be prescribed. Using the wrong antibiotic will not cure the infection and wastes medicine.

Antibiotics cannot kill viruses. Viruses are not cells: they reproduce inside the host's own cells and do not have the structures or processes that antibiotics target. This is why a doctor will not prescribe antibiotics for a cold or flu. It is also difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without damaging the body's own tissues, because the virus is hidden inside, and uses, the body's own cells.

Painkillers, such as aspirin, paracetamol and ibuprofen, and other medicines such as cough mixtures or decongestants, treat the symptoms of a disease. They can reduce pain, fever or a blocked nose, making the patient feel better while the immune system fights the infection. However, they do not kill pathogens, so they do not cure the disease.

The emergence of strains of bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics is a major concern. A resistant strain is not killed by an antibiotic that used to work against it, so infections caused by it become hard or impossible to treat. MRSA is an example of a bacterium that is resistant to several antibiotics. Resistant strains become more common when antibiotics are used, because the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce while the non-resistant ones are killed.
keyFacts: Antibiotics, such as penicillin, kill infective bacteria inside the body.
Antibiotics cure bacterial diseases because they kill the pathogen.
Specific bacteria must be treated with specific antibiotics that are effective against them.
Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases.
Antibiotics cannot kill viruses, so they do not work against viral diseases such as colds, flu or measles.
Painkillers and other medicines treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens.
It is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses without also damaging body tissues, because viruses live and reproduce inside body cells.
The emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria, such as MRSA, is of great concern.

keyTerms.definition: A medicine that kills bacteria (or stops them growing) inside the body, used to cure bacterial infections. Penicillin is an example.
A medicine, such as aspirin or paracetamol, that relieves pain (a symptom) but does not kill the pathogen causing the disease.
An effect of a disease that a person notices, such as pain, fever or a cough.
A microorganism that causes infectious disease, for example a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
When a strain of bacteria is no longer killed by an antibiotic that used to be effective against it.
A genetically different variety of a species of microorganism, for example a strain of bacteria that is resistant to an antibiotic.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: a strain of bacteria resistant to many commonly used antibiotics.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the right medicine
workedExamples.question: A patient has a sore throat caused by a virus. They ask the doctor for antibiotics. Explain why the doctor does not prescribe antibiotics and suggest what the doctor might recommend instead.
steps: Identify the type of pathogen: the sore throat is caused by a virus.
Recall that antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses, because viruses live and reproduce inside the body's cells.
So antibiotics would have no effect on the infection, and using them unnecessarily increases the chance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria developing.
The patient's immune system will destroy the virus. A painkiller such as paracetamol can relieve the pain while this happens.
workedExamples.answer: Antibiotics do not kill viruses, so they would not cure the infection, and unnecessary use encourages resistant bacteria. The doctor would suggest painkillers to treat the symptoms while the immune system fights the virus.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting an antibiotic test
workedExamples.question: Bacteria from a patient were spread on an agar plate. Paper discs soaked in antibiotics A, B and C were placed on the agar. After incubation the clear zones had diameters A = 4 mm, B = 22 mm and C = 0 mm. Which antibiotic should the doctor prescribe? Explain your answer.
steps: A clear zone forms where the antibiotic has killed the bacteria or stopped them growing.
The bigger the clear zone, the more effective the antibiotic is against this bacterium.
B has the largest clear zone (22 mm). C has no clear zone, so these bacteria are resistant to C.
This shows why specific bacteria must be treated with specific antibiotics.
workedExamples.answer: Antibiotic B, because it produced the largest clear zone, so it is most effective at killing this type of bacterium.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a percentage from resistance data
workedExamples.question: A hospital tested 2400 samples of a bacterium. 360 samples were resistant to an antibiotic. Calculate the percentage of samples that were resistant.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think antibiotics can be used to treat colds and flu.
misconceptions.right: In fact colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics cannot kill viruses. Antibiotics only work against bacteria.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think painkillers cure a disease because the patient feels better.
misconceptions.right: In fact painkillers only treat symptoms such as pain. They do not kill the pathogen; the immune system (or an antibiotic for bacteria) does that.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think people or bodies become resistant to antibiotics.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the bacteria that become resistant. A resistant strain of bacteria is not killed by the antibiotic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think any antibiotic will work against any bacterium.
misconceptions.right: In fact specific bacteria need specific antibiotics. An antibiotic that kills one type of bacterium may have no effect on another.

realWorld: Doctors may send a sample, such as a throat swab or urine sample, to a laboratory to find out which antibiotic will be effective before prescribing.
Hospitals screen patients for MRSA and use strict hand washing because infections caused by resistant strains are hard to treat.
Pharmacies sell painkillers such as paracetamol and ibuprofen without a prescription to relieve the symptoms of colds and flu, while antibiotics need a prescription.
examTips: When asked why antibiotics are not given for a viral illness, say that antibiotics cannot kill viruses. For extra marks add that unnecessary use increases antibiotic resistance.
Never write that antibiotics 'kill diseases' or 'kill viruses'. Write that antibiotics kill bacteria.
If a question asks why it is hard to develop antiviral drugs, link it to viruses being inside body cells, so the drug may damage the body's tissues.
Be precise about painkillers: they treat symptoms and do not kill pathogens, so they do not cure the disease.
In resistance questions, say the bacteria (not the patient) are resistant.
summary: Antibiotics, like penicillin, kill bacteria inside the body and cure bacterial diseases.
Specific bacteria must be treated with specific antibiotics.
Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from bacterial infections.
Painkillers and other medicines treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens.
Antiviral drugs are hard to develop without damaging body tissues.
Antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria are a serious and growing concern.

questions.question: Which type of pathogen can be killed by antibiotics?
markScheme: 1 mark: Bacteria
questions.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria inside the body. They cannot kill viruses, so they do not work against all pathogens.

questions.question: Which of these is an antibiotic?
markScheme: 1 mark: Penicillin
questions.explanation: Penicillin is an antibiotic. Aspirin and paracetamol are painkillers, and digitalis is a heart drug.

questions.question: What is the effect of taking a painkiller when you have an infection?
options: It makes you immune to the pathogen
It kills bacteria but not viruses
markScheme: 1 mark: It relieves the symptoms
questions.explanation: Painkillers treat symptoms such as pain. They do not kill pathogens and do not produce immunity.

questions.question: A person has measles, which is caused by a virus. Which treatment would help them feel better?
options: An antibiotic followed by a painkiller
markScheme: 1 mark: A painkiller
questions.explanation: Measles is viral so antibiotics will not work. A painkiller can relieve symptoms such as fever and aches while the immune system destroys the virus.

questions.question: Why is it important to identify the bacterium causing an infection before choosing an antibiotic?
options: Specific bacteria are only killed by specific antibiotics
markScheme: 1 mark: Specific bacteria are only killed by specific antibiotics
questions.explanation: Different antibiotics are effective against different bacteria, so the antibiotic must match the type of bacterium causing the infection.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses?
options: Viruses are too large for drugs to enter
Viruses reproduce inside body cells, so the drug may damage body tissues
Viruses are only found in the blood
markScheme: 1 mark: Viruses reproduce inside body cells, so the drug may damage body tissues
questions.explanation: Viruses are tiny and live inside the host's own cells. A drug that destroys them is likely to harm those cells too. Viruses do not have cell walls.

questions.question: What does 'antibiotic-resistant strain' mean?
options: A person who is not affected by antibiotics
A virus that can survive antibiotics
An antibiotic that cannot be broken down by the body
Bacteria that are not killed by an antibiotic that used to kill them
markScheme: 1 mark: Bacteria that are not killed by an antibiotic that used to kill them
questions.explanation: Resistance is a property of the bacteria, not the patient. Viruses are never killed by antibiotics, so 'resistance' does not apply to them in this sense.

questions.question: Bacteria were grown on agar with discs of four antibiotics. The clear zone diameters were: W 12 mm, X 0 mm, Y 25 mm, Z 8 mm. Which antibiotic is most effective against these bacteria?
markScheme: 1 mark: Y
questions.explanation: The largest clear zone (Y, 25 mm) shows where the most bacteria were killed or prevented from growing. X produced no clear zone so the bacteria are resistant to X.

questions.question: A doctor gives antibiotics to a patient with a viral infection 'just in case'. Which is the most likely harmful consequence?
options: The virus becomes resistant to the antibiotic
The patient becomes resistant to the antibiotic
Bacteria in the body resistant to the antibiotic survive and become more common
The antibiotic makes the viral infection worse
markScheme: 1 mark: Bacteria in the body resistant to the antibiotic survive and become more common
questions.explanation: Unnecessary antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria in the body, while any resistant bacteria survive and reproduce. Viruses and patients do not become resistant to antibiotics.

questions.question: Which pair of conditions could BOTH be cured by a suitable antibiotic?
markScheme: 1 mark: Salmonella food poisoning and gonorrhoea
questions.explanation: Salmonella and gonorrhoea are both caused by bacteria. Measles, HIV and influenza are caused by viruses, so antibiotics cannot cure them.

questions.question:
A hospital tested 2400 samples of a bacterium. 360 of the samples were resistant to an antibiotic.
Calculate the percentage of samples that were resistant.
questions.explanation: 360 ÷ 2400 = 0.15. Multiply by 100 to give 15%.

questions.question:
In one country the death rate from a bacterial disease fell from 450 per 100 000 people to 27 per 100 000 people after antibiotics were introduced.
Calculate the percentage decrease in the death rate.
questions.explanation: Decrease = 450 − 27 = 423. 423 ÷ 450 = 0.94, so the percentage decrease is 94%. This shows how greatly antibiotics reduced deaths from bacterial disease.

questions.question:
A clear zone around an antibiotic disc has a diameter of 18 mm.
Calculate the area of the clear zone using area = πr². Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
markScheme: 1 mark: radius = 9 mm
1 mark: π × 9² = 254 mm²
questions.explanation: The radius is half the diameter, 9 mm. π × 81 = 254.47, which is 254 mm² to the nearest whole number. A common error is using the diameter instead of the radius.

questions.question:
A single resistant bacterium survives a course of antibiotics. In ideal conditions it divides once every 20 minutes.
Calculate how many resistant bacteria there will be after 3 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 hours = 180 minutes, so 180 ÷ 20 = 9 divisions
1 mark: 2⁹ = 512
questions.explanation: Each division doubles the number. 9 divisions gives 1 × 2⁹ = 512 bacteria. This shows how quickly a resistant strain can become common.

questions.question: State what an antibiotic does inside the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: kills (infective) bacteria
questions.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria inside the body, which cures the bacterial disease. 'Kills germs' or 'kills viruses' would not gain the mark.

questions.question: Give one reason why a doctor would not prescribe antibiotics for the common cold.
acceptedAnswers: cold is caused by a virus
markScheme: 1 mark: colds are caused by viruses and antibiotics cannot kill viruses
questions.explanation: The common cold is viral. Antibiotics only kill bacteria, so they would have no effect.

questions.question: Name two painkillers.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: aspirin, paracetamol, ibuprofen, codeine
questions.explanation: Aspirin, paracetamol and ibuprofen are common painkillers. Penicillin is not a painkiller; it is an antibiotic.

questions.question: A student says, 'Paracetamol cured my flu.' Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: paracetamol is a painkiller that only treats/relieves symptoms
1 mark: it does not kill the (flu) virus; the immune system destroyed the virus
questions.explanation: Painkillers make you feel better but do not kill pathogens. The student recovered because their white blood cells destroyed the flu virus.

questions.question: Explain why it is difficult to develop drugs that kill viruses.
markScheme: 1 mark: viruses live and reproduce inside the body's cells
1 mark: so drugs that kill the virus are likely to damage the body's cells/tissues too
questions.explanation: Because viruses use the host's cells to reproduce, it is hard to target the virus without also harming the cells it is in.

questions.question: Antibiotics were first widely used in the 1940s. Describe the effect this has had on deaths from infectious diseases, and name the type of disease affected.
markScheme: 1 mark: deaths have been greatly reduced
1 mark: from bacterial diseases
questions.explanation: Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases. They have not reduced deaths from viral diseases directly.

questions.question: A doctor takes a swab from a patient's infected wound and sends it to a laboratory before prescribing an antibiotic. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: to identify the type of bacterium causing the infection
1 mark: so that an antibiotic effective against that specific bacterium (that it is not resistant to) can be chosen
questions.explanation: Specific bacteria must be treated with specific antibiotics. Testing also shows if the bacteria are resistant to some antibiotics.

questions.question: Explain why the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains of bacteria, such as MRSA, is of great concern.
markScheme: 1 mark: resistant bacteria are not killed by the antibiotic
1 mark: so infections are difficult or impossible to treat/cure
1 mark: so the infection can spread (e.g. in hospitals) and people may die from infections that used to be curable
questions.explanation: If antibiotics stop working, bacterial infections become as dangerous as they were before antibiotics, and very few new antibiotics are being discovered.

questions.question: Explain how using antibiotics leads to an increase in the proportion of resistant bacteria in a population.
markScheme: 1 mark: the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria
1 mark: resistant bacteria survive
1 mark: and reproduce, passing on resistance, so the resistant strain becomes more common
questions.explanation: The antibiotic removes the bacteria that it can kill, leaving the resistant ones to multiply with less competition.

questions.question: Antibiotic C produced no clear zone on a plate of bacteria from a patient. Antibiotic D produced a large clear zone. Suggest two conclusions the doctor could draw.
acceptedAnswers: C not effective against this bacterium
markScheme: 1 mark: the bacteria are resistant to C / C does not kill this type of bacterium
1 mark: D kills these bacteria so D should be prescribed
questions.explanation: No clear zone means no bacteria were killed by C. The large clear zone shows D is effective against this specific bacterium.

questions.question: Compare the use of antibiotics and painkillers in treating disease.
markScheme: Indicative content: antibiotics kill bacteria inside the body; painkillers do not kill pathogens; antibiotics cure bacterial disease; painkillers treat/relieve symptoms such as pain; antibiotics do not work on viruses; painkillers can be used for both viral and bacterial infections; specific antibiotics are needed for specific bacteria; antibiotic use can lead to resistant strains; e.g. penicillin vs aspirin/paracetamol.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of both, including what each acts on and whether it cures disease.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both medicines with little direct comparison.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good answer uses comparative words (whereas, but, both) and makes the key contrast: antibiotics kill bacteria and cure the disease, painkillers only relieve symptoms.

questions.question: A patient has a fever and sore throat. Describe how a doctor should decide on the best treatment.
markScheme: Indicative content: find out the cause (bacterium or virus), e.g. by taking a throat swab for lab testing; if viral, no antibiotics because they cannot kill viruses; recommend painkillers/rest to relieve symptoms while the immune system destroys the virus; if bacterial, identify the bacterium; test which antibiotics kill it (clear zones); prescribe a specific antibiotic it is not resistant to; painkillers can still relieve symptoms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): logical sequence covering both the viral and bacterial possibility with reasons.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. 'give antibiotics' or 'give painkillers', with limited reasoning.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that the treatment depends on the pathogen: antibiotics only for bacterial infections, and the specific antibiotic must match the bacterium.

questions.question: Explain the use of antibiotics and other medicines in treating disease. In your answer, include why antibiotics cannot be used for every infection and why their use must be controlled.
markScheme: Indicative content: antibiotics (e.g. penicillin) kill infective bacteria inside the body and cure bacterial disease; specific bacteria need specific antibiotics; antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from bacterial disease; antibiotics cannot kill viruses; viruses reproduce inside body cells so it is hard to develop antiviral drugs without damaging tissues; painkillers and other medicines (e.g. cough medicine) treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens; the immune system must destroy viruses; overuse/unnecessary use kills non-resistant bacteria leaving resistant strains to survive and reproduce; resistant strains such as MRSA are a great concern because infections become untreatable; so antibiotics should only be prescribed for serious bacterial infections and the right one chosen.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, coherent explanation covering antibiotics, other medicines, why antibiotics fail on viruses, and resistance as the reason for control.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explanation of antibiotics and painkillers with some reasoning about viruses or resistance.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple relevant statements with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers link each point to a reason: antibiotics cure because they kill bacteria; they fail on viruses because viruses are inside cells; control is needed because overuse selects resistant strains.

questions.question: Give one example of a symptom that a painkiller can treat.
markScheme: 1 mark: pain / headache / fever / aches
questions.explanation: Painkillers relieve symptoms such as pain and some, like paracetamol, also reduce fever.
